items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: When we set sail for France, Carol Dickerson of Chicago came to see us off, as he was a friend of Eugene Anderson, the ex-Cooper pianist.

ctx.x: As far as prejudice from other white musicians was concerned, this was mainly confined to the bad musicians who could not get a good job. You never heard that sort of thing from people like Gene Krupa. Even though blacks and whites belonged to the same union, they could not earn the same salaries, and even if a black orchestra got a job in a downtown district, they got paid less. It was a rotten system, but one which left the black musicians freer, to play their own music.
When we set sail for France, Carol Dickerson of Chicago came to see us off, as he was a friend of Eugene Anderson, the ex-Cooper pianist. Most of the musicians in Lucky's band had been with Cooper.

Booker Pittman, Leroy Hardy, Alfred Pratt, R.H.'Mac' Horton, Henry Goodwin, Arnold Boling and myself. I had not played with the other members but knew them and they were Bill Dillard, trumpet, Arnold Adams, guitar and Wilson Myers, bass.
